title: Portfolio Construction
tagline: From a signal to a weight: inverse volatility, volatility targeting, risk parity, drift and caps
summary: A signal is not a portfolio. This course turns signs and scores into weights: equal weight, inverse volatility, volatility targeting, and equal risk contribution. It then adds the constraints that dominate live research — drift bands, turnover budgets, tracking-error gates, drawdown breakers, long-only holdings and market-neutral budgets — and shows what each one changes in the algebra.
overview: The open library splits research into weight strategies and order strategies. This course is the weight half. A weight is a target fraction of net asset value. Getting from a vector of signals to a vector of weights is a separate model, with its own parameters, and it can dominate the signal. Two rules with the same moving-average sign can have very different paths once one of them is scaled to a volatility target.

Inverse volatility and volatility targeting both divide by a risk estimate. They answer different questions. Inverse volatility sets relative sizes so that each asset contributes a similar standalone variance. Volatility targeting scales the whole book, or a sleeve, so that a recent volatility estimate matches a chosen number. Risk parity, in the equal-risk-contribution sense, sets weights so that each position’s marginal contribution to portfolio variance is equal. A cap on a single weight is a further constraint, and it breaks the pure solution.

Rebalancing policy is part of the portfolio. Trading only at month-end, only after a weight has drifted by a stated band, or only when a tracking-error or turnover budget allows, changes turnover and therefore the cost term studied in Backtesting. A circuit breaker that flattens the book after a drawdown is a path-dependent weight, not a property of the signal.

Long-only weights live in a simplex. Market-neutral weights sum to zero, or to zero after a hedge, and need a convention for gross exposure. The course writes both feasible sets. It does not pick a portfolio for the reader.
outcomes: Map a vector of signals to a vector of weights under a stated gross-exposure and long-only or long–short constraint.
Compute inverse-volatility weights and a volatility-targeting scale, and explain the difference.
State the equal-risk-contribution condition and compute it for a diagonal covariance.
Write a drift band, a turnover budget and a tracking-error gate as constraints on the trade, not on the signal.
Define a drawdown circuit breaker as a path-dependent weight and show how it changes compound growth.
Distinguish a long-only simplex from a dollar-neutral book with a gross-exposure budget.

history.title: Variance as a portfolio objective
history.detail: Markowitz’s mean–variance problem is the ancestor of every risk budget in this course: weights chosen to control variance, subject to constraints the investor can actually hold.

history.title: Separation
history.detail: Tobin showed that, under his assumptions, every mean–variance investor holds a combination of the risk-free asset and a single tangency portfolio. Volatility targeting is a later, cruder relative of that separation.

history.title: Risk parity portfolios
history.detail: Qian’s research note argued for allocating by risk contribution rather than by capital, the idea behind the equal-risk-contribution books in this course.

history.title: The properties of equal risk contribution
history.detail: Maillard, Roncalli and Teiletche characterised equally weighted risk-contribution portfolios and their place between minimum variance and equal weight.

history.title: A single-factor hedge
history.detail: Sharpe’s CAPM supplied the beta that a later market-neutral constraint sets to zero. The model is a constraint one may impose, not a description one has to believe in full.
